unit.title: Manage self as a board member

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Mr Everton Gayle has just been appointed to the board of a statutory body. Which statement best describes the board's role?
options: To run the body's daily operations and supervise each member of staff
To set direction, oversee performance and risk, and hold management to account
To carry out the Minister's personal instructions on every staffing matter that arises
To approve every purchase and payment the body makes, whatever its size

questions.stem: A board member visits the body's Ocho Rios office and tells a clerk to change the way she files applications. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing, because board members outrank all staff in the body
Board members may give instructions only to the most senior staff
A member acting alone has no authority to direct staff; that is management's job
The clerk should have asked the member to put the instruction in an email

questions.stem: Before her first meeting, what should a new member of a public body's board read to understand its powers and purpose?
options: The body's newspaper advertisements from the past year
Only the agenda and papers for the first meeting she attends
The CVs of the other board members and of the senior management team in full
The law that set up the body, its rules, its plans and its latest reports

questions.stem: Why should a new board member take part in a formal induction?
options: To learn the body's purpose, finances, risks, duties and how the board works
To meet staff socially and choose which of the departments she will oversee herself
Because the board fee is paid only after induction is finished
So that she can skip reading board papers for the first year

questions.stem: What does the duty to act in good faith in the best interests of the body mean for a member?
options: Acting in the interests of whoever nominated or appointed the member to the board
Putting the body's interests ahead of personal, business or political interests
Voting the same way as the chair on every matter that comes to the board
Supporting management's proposals whatever the risks or the cost to the body

questions.stem: The duty of care, skill and diligence expects a board member to do what?
options: To be an expert in every subject that comes before the board
To check every invoice the body pays before it is released
To prepare, attend, ask questions and use reasonable judgement
To agree with professional advisers in every case without question

questions.stem: Which statement about the general purpose of the law on the management and accountability of public bodies is most accurate?
options: It allows board members to set their own fees and allowances freely
It removes the need for public bodies to prepare any reports
It means that board members cannot be held to account for decisions
It sets standards of care and accountability for those who govern public bodies

questions.stem: Board papers arrive a week before a meeting. A 40-page paper proposes a J$300,000,000 contract. What should a member do?
options: Read it carefully, note questions and seek missing facts before the meeting
Read only the summary page, as the full paper is mainly for management to read
Wait until the meeting and rely on the CEO's spoken briefing on the day
Vote with the majority, since others will have read the full paper

questions.stem: A member finds the financial statements in her board papers hard to understand. What is the best response?
options: Say nothing, so that she does not look unprepared
Ask the finance officer or chair for a briefing and build her skills
Leave all financial matters to the member who is an accountant, and say nothing
Abstain on every item that involves money for the whole of her term

questions.stem: During debate, a member doubts the cost figures in a proposal, but the rest of the board seems in favour. What should she do?
options: Stay quiet, because disagreeing would harm the board's unity
Leave the meeting before the vote so that she is not involved
Raise her concern clearly and ask for it to be minuted if not resolved
Tell the press after the meeting that she believes the cost figures are wrong

questions.stem: The board makes a decision that a member voted against. What is his duty afterwards?
options: To speak publicly against the decision in order to protect his reputation
To refuse to take part in any board work linked to the decision
To ask staff to delay carrying out the decision until the next meeting
To support it publicly as a board decision, or resign if he truly cannot

questions.stem: Which situation is a conflict of interest for a board member?
options: Her husband's firm is bidding for a contract the board will award
She disagrees with the CEO about the body's marketing plan for next year
She has more years of experience than the other members
She lives in the same parish as the body's head office

questions.stem: Ms Simone Barrett sees that next week's agenda includes renting a building owned by her cousin. What should she do?
options: Say nothing unless another member asks her directly about the building
Declare the interest as early as possible and follow the board's rules on it
Speak in favour of the rental, as she knows the building well
Ask her cousin to lower the rent so that the deal looks fair

questions.stem: A member has declared a financial interest in an item. What does good practice usually expect of her during that item?
options: To stay and vote, since she has declared the interest openly
To stay and speak but not vote, so the board has her views
To leave the room for the discussion and vote, as recorded in the minutes
To chair that item, so that it is handled quickly

questions.stem: Why do many boards keep a register of members' interests, updated each year?
options: To decide how much each member will be paid for attending board meetings
To show the public which members are the wealthiest
To let staff contact members about private business
To make interests known in advance so conflicts are spotted

questions.stem: A member is a partner in a law firm. The body wants to hire outside lawyers. Which step is most appropriate?
options: Declare the interest and take no part in the choice; the firm competes under the rules
Recommend her own firm, as she knows it does good work at a fair price
Ask the CEO to appoint her firm without competition to save time
Resign from the board at once so that her firm can bid

questions.stem: Which is an example of a non-financial conflict of interest?
options: A member owning shares in a supplier
A member's close friend applying for the CEO post
A member being paid a board fee
A member claiming travel costs

questions.stem: A firm that hopes to win a contract sends a board member a hamper and tickets to an overseas cricket match. What should he do?
options: Keep the hamper but return the tickets
Accept both, as they arrived at Christmas time when gifts are normal
Decline, and report the offer under the code of conduct
Give the tickets to a member of staff

questions.stem: A friend asks a board member what the board decided about job cuts before staff have been told. What should she say?
options: Tell the friend in confidence, as long as no names are given
Give a hint, so that the friend is not left wondering
Tell the friend, since the decision has already been made
Explain that board matters are confidential until announced

questions.stem: A member keeps printed board papers on a café table while he takes a phone call. What principle is he putting at risk?
options: Keeping board information secure and confidential
Collective responsibility of all members for each board decision
The board's duty to prepare a yearly report
Value for money in the body's spending

questions.stem: A member learns at a board meeting that the body will soon buy land in a certain area. He plans to buy a plot nearby first. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, as he is buying with his own money
He would be using confidential board information for personal gain
He should ask the CEO's permission before buying, then go ahead with the purchase
He should buy the plot only through a relative

questions.stem: A journalist phones a board member for comment on a controversy at the body. What should the member usually do?
options: Give a full interview, as members have a right to speak
Give a comment 'off the record' so that she is not named
Refer the journalist to the chair or the agreed spokesperson
Post her own view on social media later that day

questions.stem: A board member is also active in a political party. How should this affect his board work?
options: He should steer contracts to firms that support his party, when he can
He should use board meetings to promote party policy
He should resign from the party before any meeting
He should keep party interests out of his board decisions

questions.stem: The Minister responsible for a public body phones a member privately and asks him to block a staff appointment. What should the member do?
options: Explain that he acts through the board, and tell the chair about the call
Agree, as the Minister appointed him and he must follow the Minister's wishes
Tell the CEO to cancel the appointment at once
Ignore the call and say nothing to anyone

questions.stem: What is the best working relationship between board members and the CEO?
options: Members manage the CEO's daily diary and tasks
Constructive challenge and support, with clear roles
Members avoid all contact with the CEO between meetings
Members accept every proposal the CEO brings

questions.stem: What does it mean for a board member to exercise independent judgement?
options: Refusing to listen to the views of any other members of the board
Always voting against management to show strength
Forming her own view on the evidence, free of undue pressure
Making decisions alone without going to meetings

questions.stem: A board member attended 7 of the board's 10 meetings this year. What was her attendance rate?
A member's new job means he will miss most board meetings for the next year. What is the responsible action?
options: Discuss it with the chair and consider stepping down
Keep the seat and send a staff member in his place
Keep the seat and vote by phone without reading papers
Say nothing and hope the board does not notice

questions.stem: A board meets 10 times a year for 3 hours, and each meeting needs about 4 hours of reading. The member also sits on a committee that needs 20 hours a year. How many hours a year should she plan?
options: 50 hours
90 hours
70 hours
34 hours

questions.stem: A member is invited to join a third board while already serving on two. What should she think about first?
options: Whether the new board pays a higher fee than the two she is on now
Whether the new board meets in Kingston
Whether she has the time and has no conflict with the other boards
Whether her friends sit on the new board

questions.stem: A member with an accounting background is asked to join the audit committee. What should she understand about her role there?
options: That she takes over the internal auditor's job
That she approves each payment the body makes
That she may change the accounts herself
That she helps the board oversee financial reporting, controls and audit

questions.stem: A member notices that the risk register has not been updated for a year, though a hurricane damaged two offices. What should she do?
options: Raise it at the board and ask management to review the risks and report back
Rewrite the risk register herself and send it straight to staff to use from now on
Say nothing, as risk is a matter for management alone
Ask the insurer to update the register

questions.stem: A board relies on a legal opinion when it makes a decision. Why is it still important for each member to understand the advice?
options: Because members must give legal advice to staff
Because members keep responsibility and should rely on advice only after weighing it
Because the lawyer's opinion is never relevant
Because members must sign the lawyer's bill

questions.stem: Why do many public bodies arrange liability insurance for directors and board members?
options: So that members can ignore their duties without risk
So that members need not attend meetings
To protect members who act honestly and with care against certain legal costs
To pay members a bonus if the body does well

questions.stem: A member suspects that a senior manager is misusing funds. What should she do?
options: Investigate on her own by questioning junior staff
Accuse the manager at a staff meeting
Wait until the next audit in eighteen months
Raise it promptly with the chair or audit committee, following the body's procedures

questions.stem: Why does a public body adopt a code of conduct for its board members?
options: To set the standards of behaviour expected and how breaches are handled
To list the dates and places of all the board meetings for the coming year
To describe the body's products and services
To set out the pay of the body's staff

questions.stem: At a meeting, a member mocks a colleague's question as 'stupid'. What principle of board conduct has he broken?
options: Collective responsibility
Respect and courtesy towards fellow members
Confidentiality of board papers
The duty to declare interests

questions.stem: A member wants to post on social media about a board debate that went badly. What should she do?
options: Post it, but leave out the other members' names so that no one is embarrassed
Post it, as her account is private
Not post board discussions; follow the body's communication policy
Post only a photo of the board papers

questions.stem: Why should a board member assess her own performance each year?
options: Because the board fee depends on the score she gives herself
To prove to the Minister that she should be chair
To find faults in other members' work
To see her strengths and gaps and plan her development

questions.stem: Which question is most useful in a board member's self-assessment?
options: Did I prepare well, add value in debate and act within my duties?
Did I speak more often and for longer than the other members of the board?
Did I win most of the votes I took part in?
Did the CEO agree with me on most matters?

questions.stem: A member wants to improve her understanding of governance. Which plan is most suitable?
options: Rely on what she learned in her own career
Take a governance course, read guidance and learn from experienced members
Ask staff to explain each matter to her during meetings
Wait until the board's yearly retreat

questions.stem: The chair asks each member to complete a board evaluation survey. How should a member approach it?
options: Give the highest marks to avoid upsetting the chair
Refuse, as evaluation is only for staff
Give honest, specific and constructive feedback
Use it to complain about a member she dislikes

questions.stem: A member serving on four boards feels exhausted and is falling behind on papers. What is the best step?
options: Keep going and skim the papers at the meetings
Ask another member to read the papers for him
Stop attending without telling anyone
Review his commitments and reduce them to a level he can manage well

questions.stem: A member decides to resign from a public body's board. What should she do?
options: Resign in writing as the rules require and return all board papers
Stop attending meetings, and keep all her board papers as a personal record
Announce it first on social media
Ask a friend to take her seat at the next meeting

questions.stem: To whom is the board of a public body ultimately accountable for how it uses public money?
options: Only to the body's own staff and to the union that represents them
Through the Minister and Parliament to the public
Only to its largest suppliers
To no one, once the budget is approved

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What record, kept by the board secretary, lists each member's business, financial and other interests? (Three or four words.)
What one-word term means to withdraw from a discussion or decision because of a conflict of interest?
What one-word term describes the duty of trust a board member owes: to act honestly, in good faith and in the body's best interests? (Often followed by 'duty'.)
What two-word term names the principle that all members stand behind a board decision once it is made?
What is the planned introduction a new board member receives to the body, its work and the board's ways called?
A public body's board adopts a document listing its standards of honesty, respect and integrity, and how breaches will be handled. What is it usually called? (Three words.)
A board's rules require each member to attend at least 75% of its 12 meetings a year. What is the fewest meetings a member must attend?
What one-word term describes a conflict of interest that involves money or financial gain? (Often used with 'interest'.)
What two-word term names the law passed to set up a statutory body and give it its powers?
What one-word term names the duty not to share board discussions and papers that have not been made public?
A board meets 6 times a year. Each meeting takes 3 hours plus 5 hours of reading. How many hours a year does this need?
What insurance protects board members acting honestly against certain claims over their decisions? (Use the usual name or its letters.)
What two-word term names the yearly review of how well the board and its members have performed?
What term describes a member who has no material business or family link with the body or its management? (One word, used before 'member' or 'director'.)
What two-word term names a situation in which a fair-minded observer might think a member's judgement could be affected, even if it is not? (Starts with 'perceived' or 'apparent'.)

essays.stem: Explain the main duties of a member of a public body's board, and how a member can show that she is meeting them.
essays.modelAnswer: A board member must act honestly and in good faith in the best interests of the body, not for herself, her business, her party or whoever appointed her. She must use her powers only for their proper purpose, within the law that set up the body and its rules. She owes a duty of care, skill and diligence: to prepare, attend, ask questions and use reasonable judgement. She must avoid conflicts of interest, declare any she has and withdraw where required, and must not use her position or board information for personal gain. She must keep board matters confidential and support board decisions collectively. As a member of a public body, she must also help the board account for public money in line with the law on the management and accountability of public bodies. She shows she is meeting these duties by reading papers, asking informed questions that are recorded, keeping her declarations up to date, attending regularly, completing training and taking part honestly in self-assessment and board evaluation.
markingPoints: Good faith in the body's best interests and proper purpose
Care, skill and diligence: preparation, attendance, questions, judgement
Avoiding and declaring conflicts and not using information for gain
Confidentiality, collective responsibility and public accountability
Shows evidence of meeting duties (records, declarations, attendance, training)

essays.stem: Compare the role of the board with the role of management in a statutory body, and explain why a member must respect the difference.
essays.modelAnswer: The board sets the body's direction within its law and government policy: it approves the strategy, the budget and major policies, appoints and oversees the CEO, monitors performance, risks and controls, and accounts for results. Management, led by the CEO, runs the body day to day: it plans and carries out the work, manages staff, spends within the budget and reports to the board. In short, the board steers and checks; management rows. A member must respect this because the board acts only as a body, through its decisions, and an individual member has no authority to direct staff. If members step into management, staff receive mixed instructions, the CEO cannot be held to account for results the board interfered with, and the board loses the distance it needs to judge management fairly. Respecting the line does not mean being passive: members should ask searching questions, request information through the CEO or chair, and challenge proposals at meetings, while leaving the running of the body to management.
markingPoints: Board role: direction, strategy, budget, policy, oversight of CEO and risk
Management role: running operations, staff, spending and reporting
A member alone has no authority to direct staff
Explains the harms of crossing the line (confusion, accountability, objectivity)
Members still challenge and seek information through proper channels

essays.stem: Ms Barrett's cousin owns a building that the board is considering renting for J$2,400,000 a year. Explain what Ms Barrett should do, step by step, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: As soon as she sees the item, Ms Barrett should tell the chair or the board secretary in writing that her cousin owns the building, even though she does not benefit directly, because a close family link could affect, or appear to affect, her judgement. She should also check that the relationship is in the register of interests. At the meeting she should declare the interest when declarations are called for, so that it is minuted. She should not try to influence other members, before or during the meeting, and should not pass any information about the board's thinking to her cousin. Following the board's rules, she should leave the room for the discussion and vote, and the minutes should record that she left and returned. Afterwards she should take no part in managing the lease. These steps protect the body from a decision that could be challenged, protect public money, and protect her own reputation, since the test is whether a fair-minded observer would think her judgement could be affected.
markingPoints: Declares early, in writing, to the chair or secretary, and updates the register
Declares at the meeting so it is minuted
Does not influence members or share board information with the cousin
Leaves for the discussion and vote, recorded in the minutes, and stays out of managing the lease
Explains why: protects the decision, public money and her reputation (appearance test)

essays.stem: Describe how a board member should prepare for a board meeting, and justify why preparation matters.
essays.modelAnswer: When the papers arrive, the member should set aside enough time to read them in full, not only the summaries. For each item she should ask: what is the board being asked to decide, is the information enough, what are the risks and costs, and does it fit the strategy and budget? She should check the minutes and action log of the last meeting to see whether promised actions were done. She should note questions and, for complex or factual points, send them to the board secretary or CEO beforehand so that answers are ready. She should check the agenda for any item where she has an interest and declare it early. She should look up anything she does not understand, such as a financial term. She should keep the papers secure. Preparation matters because the duty of care requires members to make informed decisions; a member who has not read the papers cannot challenge a weak proposal. It also uses meeting time well and shows respect for colleagues and staff who wrote the papers.
markingPoints: Reads full papers in good time and identifies the decision asked for
Tests information, risks, costs and fit with strategy
Checks previous minutes and actions; sends questions in advance
Checks for conflicts and keeps papers secure
Justifies preparation by the duty of care and effective meetings

essays.stem: A board member strongly disagrees with a board decision to close a rural office. Evaluate her options and recommend what she should do.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the decision, she should have stated her concerns clearly at the meeting with evidence, and she may ask for her disagreement to be recorded in the minutes. Once the decision is made, her options are to accept it and support it, to criticise it publicly, to keep raising it inside the board, or to resign. Criticising it publicly would break collective responsibility and confidentiality, damage trust within the board and confuse staff and the public, so it is not proper. Raising it again inside the board is acceptable if new facts appear, for example new data on the effect on rural customers, and she may ask the board to review how the closure is handled, such as through mobile services. Resigning is right only if the matter is so serious that she cannot in conscience support the board, for example if she believes the decision is unlawful. I recommend that she accepts the decision publicly, makes sure her view is minuted, and uses proper board channels to monitor its effects and propose improvements.
markingPoints: States concerns before the decision and has dissent minuted
Rejects public criticism as breaking collective responsibility and confidentiality
Allows raising it again internally with new evidence
Considers resignation for matters of conscience or legality
Gives a clear recommendation

essays.stem: Explain the risks to a board member of accepting gifts and hospitality, and describe how she should handle offers.
essays.modelAnswer: Gifts and hospitality can create a sense of obligation, even when the member believes she is not influenced. If the giver is a supplier or bidder, or someone affected by a board decision, accepting can look like a reward or an attempt to buy influence, which damages public trust and may break the code of conduct and anti-corruption law. It can also make a later decision open to challenge. The member should know the body's rules on gifts. As a general approach, she should refuse any gift or hospitality from anyone bidding for work or seeking a decision, especially during a procurement. Small items of token value, such as a branded pen at a conference, may be allowed if the rules permit. Any offer, accepted or not, should be recorded in the gifts register and reported to the board secretary. If she is unsure, she should ask the chair before accepting. She should never accept cash or anything given privately. The test is whether a reasonable observer would think her judgement could be affected.
markingPoints: Explains obligation and the appearance of influence
Notes effects on trust, legality and challenge to decisions
Refuses gifts from bidders or those seeking decisions
Records and reports offers; asks when unsure; never accepts cash
Applies the reasonable observer test

essays.stem: Plan how you, as a board member, would assess your own performance over a year and build a development plan.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from what is expected of me: the duties in the law and the code of conduct, the role description for members and any skills the board asked me to bring, such as finance. I would rate myself against clear questions: Did I read the papers in time? Did I attend and stay for full meetings? Did my questions add value? Did I declare interests promptly? Did I keep confidentiality and respect colleagues? Did I contribute to committee work? I would support my view with evidence: my attendance rate, the minutes of my contributions and feedback from the chair. I would ask the chair for a short one-to-one review and take part honestly in the board's evaluation. From this I would list two or three strengths and two or three gaps, for example a weak grasp of the body's risk framework. My development plan would set specific actions, such as a governance course, a briefing from the internal auditor and a site visit, with dates, and I would review it at the next evaluation.
markingPoints: Uses the expected duties and role description as the standard
Rates herself on preparation, attendance, contribution and conduct
Uses evidence and feedback from the chair and board evaluation
Identifies strengths and gaps
Sets specific development actions with dates and a review

essays.stem: A Minister privately asks a board member to make sure a contract goes to a certain firm. Explain how the member should respond and why.
essays.modelAnswer: The member should politely refuse to act on a private request and explain that board decisions on contracts are made collectively, under the procurement rules and the law on public bodies, on the basis of fair evaluation. He should not promise anything or try to influence other members or staff. He should make a written note of the call, with the date and what was said, and tell the chair promptly so that the board can decide how to respond formally, for example through a letter from the chair. If the matter involves possible wrongdoing, the chair may need to refer it to the proper authorities. The member should declare the contact if the contract comes before the board. He should act this way because his duty is to the body and the public interest, not to the person who appointed him. Giving in would break the procurement rules, expose the body to legal challenge and loss, damage public trust and put the member at personal risk. Ministers may set general policy through proper channels, but not direct specific contracts privately.
markingPoints: Refuses politely, explaining collective decisions under procurement rules
Does not influence others or promise anything
Records the call and tells the chair promptly
Explains duty to the body and public interest, not the appointer
Notes the risks of giving in and the proper channel for ministerial policy

essays.stem: A member serves on two boards and has a demanding full-time job. Recommend how she should manage her time and commitments so that she meets her duties.
essays.modelAnswer: She should first work out the real time each role needs. For example, a board that meets 10 times a year for 3 hours, with 4 hours of reading per meeting and 20 hours of committee work, needs about 90 hours a year, before travel and site visits. She should add the meeting dates for both boards to her calendar at the start of the year and block reading time two or three days before each meeting. She should agree with her employer how board work fits with her job. She should prioritise: attend and prepare fully for core meetings, and take on committee roles only where she has the time and the skills. If a period of heavy work is coming, she should tell the chairs early. She should not accept a third board, or a chair role, until she has shown she can manage the first two well. If she finds she cannot prepare properly, she should discuss stepping down from one board, because a member who cannot prepare cannot meet her duty of care. She should also protect her own wellbeing.
markingPoints: Estimates the time each role needs
Plans the year: meeting dates and blocked reading time
Agrees fit with employer and prioritises roles and committees
Communicates early with chairs and avoids overcommitting
Considers stepping down if duties cannot be met, and protects wellbeing

essays.stem: A board member receives an anonymous letter claiming that the CEO is hiring relatives. Describe what the member should and should not do.
essays.modelAnswer: The member should treat the letter seriously but not assume it is true. She should not investigate on her own, question staff, confront the CEO privately or share the letter with others, because that could harm an innocent person, alert anyone involved, damage evidence and break the procedures. She should promptly pass the letter to the chair, or to the audit committee chair if the chair is close to the matter, and keep a note of when she received it and what she did. The board should then follow its whistleblowing or investigation procedure: decide who will look into it, perhaps internal audit or an independent investigator, and set terms of reference. Both the person who raised the concern and the CEO must be treated fairly, and the CEO must have a chance to respond. The member should keep the matter confidential and declare any interest, such as a close friendship with the CEO. When the report comes to the board, she should judge it on the evidence.
markingPoints: Takes it seriously without assuming it is true
Does not investigate alone, confront or share the letter
Passes it promptly to the chair or audit committee chair and keeps a note
Board follows the proper procedure, with fairness to both sides
Keeps confidentiality, declares any interest and judges on evidence

practical1.title: Prepare a board member induction guide and personal development plans
practical1.brief: Your group has been asked by the chair of a public body (the assessor gives you a scenario, such as a parish development agency or a water board) to prepare a short induction guide for new board members. The guide must cover: the board's role compared with management; the member's main duties; conflicts of interest, with a declaration form and a register entry; gifts, confidentiality and speaking to the media; time commitment, with a worked estimate of hours per year; and how members are evaluated. Give each member a named role: editor (plans and checks the whole guide), duties writer, conflicts writer (designs the declaration form and register page), conduct writer (gifts, confidentiality, media and social media), and in a group of five a development officer (self-assessment form and time estimate). After the guide is finished, each member completes a one-page self-assessment and development plan as if they were a new member, using the group's form. Present the guide to the assessor, each member explaining their section.
materials: Computer with word processor and printer, or paper and pens
photos: The plan for the guide with each member's name and section
The section on the board's role and members' duties
The conflict-of-interest declaration form and register page
The conduct section and the time commitment estimate
The completed self-assessment and development plans (personal comments covered if a member wishes)
checklist: Carried out a named role and wrote their own section
Explains the board's role and the member's duties accurately and in plain words
Declaration form and register capture the interest, the item and the action taken
Conduct section gives correct guidance on gifts, confidentiality and media
Time estimate is worked out correctly
Completed a realistic self-assessment and development plan with dated actions
Explained their section clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Use a made-up public body and names; do not describe any real board member
Self-assessments are seen only by the member and the assessor
Keep comments about duties and conduct general, not about real people
Share the work fairly and take a short break each hour

practical2.title: Handle conduct and conflict scenarios as board members
practical2.brief: Each member of your group is a board member of a made-up statutory body. The assessor gives each member a different sealed scenario card, for example: a relative bidding for a contract; a supplier's offer of hospitality; a journalist's call; a Minister's private request; a friend asking about a confidential decision; or an anonymous complaint about the CEO. In turn, each member reads their card aloud, explains in 3 to 5 minutes what they will do and why, and completes the written evidence the situation needs (a declaration of interest, a gifts register entry, a note to the chair, or a file note of a call). The rest of the group question the member and add points. Then the group role-plays a 15-minute extract of a board meeting at which one member declares an interest and withdraws, and another raises a concern properly, while a member acting as secretary records it. Finally, the group writes a one-page 'lessons for board members' sheet. Photograph each stage.
materials: Sealed scenario cards from the assessor (one per member)
